clue.text: Bill's relative keeps Charlie company

indicators.note: To keep someone company is to stay wrapped around them, so 'keeps' asks one word to hold the others inside it.

parts.note: an aunt is a relative, and she is the word doing the keeping
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
co = company, as in the name of a firm

explanation.surface: Someone's aunt is sitting with a man called Charlie so that he is not left on his own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' does two jobs at once: it is the CO the wordplay wants, and it is what makes 'keeps Charlie company' read as a kindness rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill and an account are the same demand for money — the restaurant's bill is the account you settle.

clue.text: A very large rugby player breaks fitting

indicators.note: A prop breaking through a line ends up in the middle of it, so 'breaks' puts one word inside another.

parts.note: the clue's own A starts the assembly
OS = outsize, the label on very large clothing
a prop is the front-row forward who props up the scrum

explanation.surface: An enormous forward smashes a fixture, the sort of damage a heavy pack leaves behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fitting' is the trap's other half: in the surface it is a plumber's fixture, a thing a big man can break, and the answer needs it as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitting is the adjective sense — a remark that is fitting suits the moment exactly, nothing to do with plumbing.

clue.text: Rich red and variety of canapes might do inside

indicators.note: A variety of a thing is that thing in a different arrangement, which is what these letters are asked for.
'Inside' says the party word is not tacked on the end but buried in the middle of the shuffled letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters
a do is a social — the British word for a party you get invited to

explanation.surface: A deep red wine and a few little canapés would do nicely for people entertaining at home.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a jibe rather than a description: someone who votes left and lives well. 'Do' is the British word for a party, which lets 'might do inside' read as catering.
explanation.definitionFit: The sneering name for a wealthy person with left-wing politics — 'red' for the politics, 'rich' for the lifestyle.

clue.text: You, me and that Girl Guide

parts.note: you and me together are us
the girl being pointed at is her

explanation.surface: A Girl Guide is being pointed out to two people standing together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Girl Guide' is the trap: the capital G makes the two words look like one thing, and the definition is only the second of them.
explanation.definitionFit: To guide someone to their seat is exactly what the answer's verb means — the wedding sense of showing people where to go.

clue.text: Shows guys making American jeans

indicators.note: the American letter is made into jeans, so one piece of the word for guys is swapped for another

parts.note: to guy someone is to mock or tease them
Levi is the jeans brand (Levi's), by the setter's licence in the singular

explanation.surface: Someone reports that a TV programme features men manufacturing denim in the USA.
explanation.walkthrough: To guy is to mock, so 'guys' is TEASES; 'making' turns its A (American) into LEVI (jeans), giving TE-LEVI-SES. Bloggers noted the brand is strictly Levi's.
explanation.definitionFit: To televise something is to broadcast it, so a network that televises a programme shows it on screen.

clue.text: Aussie rugby international's fool to tackle All Blacks' biggest units

indicators.note: A rugby tackle wraps your arms right round the man, so 'to tackle' asks one word to go round another.

parts.note: a wally is a fool in British slang

indicators.note: The biggest version of a letter is its capital, so a name's biggest units are the initials printed large.

parts.note: the two capitals in the name of New Zealand's rugby side, taken as they stand

explanation.surface: An Australian player throws himself at the heaviest men in the New Zealand pack.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one pack of forwards taking on another, and the men it names are New Zealanders while the answer is an Australian — the definition sits right at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wallabies are Australia's national rugby union team, so the answer names one of their players — the team nickname used of a single man.

clue.text: Returning uncooked iron-enriched biscuit

indicators.note: Something returning comes back the way it went, so the letters beside it are read the other way about.
Food enriched with iron has the iron put into it, so 'enriched' asks for the metal's symbol to go inside.

parts.note: raw food is uncooked, and these three letters are then read backwards
Fe is iron's chemical symbol

explanation.surface: A diner sends back something from the tea tray for being underdone, iron supplement and all.
explanation.walkthrough: Breakfast cereals really are iron-enriched, which is what lets the surface pose as a nutrition label instead of an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A wafer is a very thin crisp biscuit, the sort served beside ice cream — a plain synonym in the baking sense.

clue.text: These parts of 26 will get her everywhere

parts.words: These parts of 26 will get her
parts.note: 26 across is HORSE; its leftmost letter H, its rightmost E and its central R together spell her

explanation.surface: A rider is told that the right bits of a horse will carry her anywhere she wants.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as instructions: the left, right and centre letters of HORSE (26 across) are H, E and R, which spell 'her'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something happening in all directions at once, scattered all over the place.

clue.text: Case of protestor getting into trouble in days immediately following March

indicators.note: one piece gets into another, so it is placed inside it

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer shell, its first and last letters

parts.note: its outside letters are P and R

explanation.surface: A demonstrator lands in difficulty during the days just after March.
explanation.definitionFit: The month that comes straight after March in the calendar is a run of thirty days.

clue.text: Bore seeing almost all eyelids sadly, drooping at the start

indicators.note: the eyelids are in a sorry state, which signals that their letters are jumbled
almost all of the word means its last letter is dropped

parts.note: the word as written, losing its final S

indicators.note: only the letter at the start of drooping is used

parts.note: its first letter is D

explanation.surface: Someone tired looks at sagging, weary eyelids.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost all' drops the S of eyelids, 'sadly' rearranges EYELID into YIELDE, and 'at the start' takes D from drooping.
explanation.definitionFit: Bore is the past tense of bear, as in a tree that bore fruit, which means produced or gave.

clue.text: Stretch and run, feel pain after cycling

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: the word is cycled, its last letter moving round to the front

parts.note: to ache is to feel pain

explanation.surface: A runner stretches, jogs and feels sore once the bike ride is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's bike ride is a red herring: 'cycling' is the instruction to rotate the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretch and reach are synonyms for extending an arm or a range as far as it will go.

clue.text: Person getting break on QI?

parts.note: in insurance and in headlines a life is a person: the crash claimed five lives
to force a door is to break it open

explanation.surface: A contestant gets a lucky break on a television quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: QI is a British comedy quiz programme, which is what the italics want you to see; the same two letters are the Chinese word the definition needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Qi is the Chinese name for the vital energy said to flow through a living body, and the answer is the plain English phrase for it.

clue.text: This could make Liam hide?

parts.note: read as wordplay, a paper (MAIL, as in the Daily Mail) turned over gives the name Liam

explanation.surface: It asks what might make a man called Liam go into hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as instructions: PAPER is MAIL, the British newspaper, and OVER turns it backwards into LIAM.
explanation.definitionFit: To paper over cracks is to conceal problems superficially, so the phrasal verb means cover up.

clue.text: Determined game was up

parts.note: RU is rugby union, the game as it is abbreviated on fixture lists
a side that was up in a match led it

explanation.surface: Someone works out that the contest is lost and the game is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The game was up' is the idiom the surface leans on, meaning the end has come, and the wordplay needs 'game' and 'was up' read as two separate things.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge who ruled on a point determined it — the past tense of handing down a decision, not the sense of being strong-willed.

clue.text: Suit (gent's) regularly discounted in Marks

indicators.note: Discounting at a regular interval throws away every second letter, leaving the first, third, fifth and so on.

parts.note: the odd-numbered letters of SUIT GENTS, counting the brackets out

explanation.surface: A gentleman's suit is on sale at a cut price in a high-street shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks' in the surface is Marks & Spencer, the British chain where a suit might be discounted, and the definition needs it as plain marks instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Signs are marks: the marks on a page or in the sky are the things you read a meaning from, and both words are plural.

clue.text: See 2
Stunned as Bambi became this grand deer with animation

indicators.note: Something done with animation is done with lively movement, and letters moved about that lively will not stay in the order given.

parts.note: the fawn of the film grows into a stag by the end of it
G is the standard abbreviation for grand
the four letters of DEER rearranged

explanation.surface: Bambi's growing up into a full-grown animal is one of the great moments in the cartoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With animation' means liveliness and points at the film in the same breath, which is how the anagram signal disappears into the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To be staggered is to be stunned — the shock sense of the word, not the one about walking unsteadily.

clue.text: See 6
Player of music ultimately wanting in on Mardi Gras parties

indicators.note: A word that is ultimately wanting is missing its final letter, and here every word in the list loses its last one.
To part is to split up, so 'parties' says the letters break apart and re-form rather than naming a night out.

parts.note: IN, ON, MARDI and GRAS each lose their final letter, leaving nine letters to shuffle

explanation.surface: Someone is angling for an invitation to the carnival balls in New Orleans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting in on' reads as one phrase — angling for an invitation — and it is really two instructions with a word boundary through the middle, which is where the four short words come from.
explanation.definitionFit: The old cabinet that housed a wireless and a record player in one piece of furniture is what the definition points at.

clue.text: 90 got through on buzzer to go to the loo

indicators.note: In an across clue one thing 'on' another leans against it from the right, so the buzzer's letters are written first.

parts.note: a bee is the thing that buzzes
ninety in Roman numerals: ten short of a hundred
to get through a supply is to use it up

explanation.surface: A quiz contestant reaches 90 by buzzing in, then asks for a comfort break.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a game show, so '90 got through on buzzer' reads as a score; the answer is the British schoolroom request for permission to leave the room.
explanation.definitionFit: In a British school you ask to be excused when you need the lavatory, a polite formula that has come to mean that errand and no other.

clue.text: From memory, Spooner's greeting a Simpson

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, which signals the swap here

parts.note: hi is a greeting, said aloud with the same vowel as by
Bart is a character in The Simpsons; with the swapped consonant it is said like heart

explanation.surface: Someone recites, from memory, a hello to a cartoon character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooner's' swaps the opening sounds: HI BART becomes BY HEART, with the words heard rather than spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: To know something by heart is to have learnt it so well that it can be recited without notes.

clue.text: Edward VI possibly died thrashing about on reflection

indicators.note: Thrashing about goes round and round, so 'about' asks the thrashing word to wrap itself around the letter beside it.
A reflection shows a thing the other way round, so the assembled letters are read backwards.

parts.note: a rout is a thrashing, one side beaten out of sight
d = died, as on a gravestone or in a family tree

explanation.surface: A guess at how the boy king met his end, thrashing about in his last hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On reflection' means thinking again in the surface and a mirror in the wordplay, which is the only reason the two readings sit together so quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward VI belonged to the royal house that ruled England from 1485 to 1603, so the king is one example of the dynasty and 'possibly' flags it.

clue.text: Short song by Queen covered by extremely raucous rappers?

indicators.note: one piece is covered by another, so it sits inside it
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: its outside letters are R and S

indicators.note: short means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: a hymn is a religious song
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword Queen

explanation.surface: A clipped tune sung by a monarch is drowned out by loud hip-hop artists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covered by' puts the shortened song plus ER inside R and S, the extremes of raucous; the question mark flags rappers as one kind of versifier.
explanation.definitionFit: Rappers speak in rhyming verse, so the question mark admits they are an example of versifiers.

clue.text: News article on ambassador to add colour?

indicators.note: In an across clue one thing 'on' another sits to its right, so the ambassador's letters are written first.

parts.note: HE is His or Her Excellency, the style an ambassador is addressed by
N is the abbreviation for new, and doubling a letter makes it plural, the way pp means pages
A is an article, taken as the word itself

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about an ambassador, written to brighten up the day's coverage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Add colour to a story' is the surface's idiom for livening it up, and the answer needs the words literally — dye on hair, not detail in a report.
explanation.definitionFit: The reddish plant dye is used as a verb for what it does: put it on hair and you add colour to it, which the question mark flags as loose.

clue.text: Snooping on revolutionary agreed in retrospect

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns around, so the word is read backwards
looking back means reading the word from the end

parts.note: yes is the word of agreement

explanation.surface: Someone is spying on a rebel who in hindsight said yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' turns ON into NO, and 'in retrospect' turns YES into SEY.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosey person pries into others' business, which is exactly what someone snooping is doing.

clue.text: Penny read about politician being prone to stalking

indicators.note: Letters sent about are sent every which way, so the four beside it come back in a different order.

parts.note: p = penny, the coin's abbreviation on a price tag
the four letters of READ rearranged
a Tory is a British Conservative

explanation.surface: Penny reads an article about a politician with a habit of following people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny read about' looks like a woman with a newspaper and is three separate instructions; 'about' is the shuffling signal, not the subject of her reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A predatory animal stalks its prey, so 'prone to stalking' names the very habit the adjective describes.

clue.text: Discussed aircraft's manifest

indicators.note: Something discussed is spoken rather than written, so the answer is what the other word sounds like, not how it is spelt.

parts.note: an aircraft is a plane, and said aloud it can be written a second way

explanation.surface: The cargo list of an aircraft is being talked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manifest' is the trap: on an aircraft it is the cargo list, a noun, while the definition wants the adjective meaning obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: Something plain is manifest — out in the open, obvious at a glance — rather than the flat-ground or unadorned senses.

clue.text: For this special purpose, stir round hot and cold

indicators.note: Stirring goes round in circles, so 'round' asks the stir word to close around the letter that follows it.

parts.note: an ado is a stir, a fuss — much ado about nothing
H is the hot tap
C is the cold tap, the two of them labelled that way on every sink

explanation.surface: A recipe step: stir the mixture with hot and cold water to hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters come straight off a pair of taps, which is how 'hot and cold' can sit in a cooking instruction without looking like wordplay at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin tag translates as 'for this': a committee formed this way exists for one particular purpose and nothing else.

clue.text: Alan Turing's beginning to comprehend Nazis' smart tech he attacks

definitions.note: The definition is a clause and the answer a noun; setters use 'he attacks' as shorthand for 'the one who attacks'.

parts.note: the mathematician's first name, taken as it stands

indicators.note: To comprehend something is to take it in and hold it, so the name outside closes around what follows.

parts.note: the opening letter of the surname
SS is the Nazi party's paramilitary corps
AI is artificial intelligence, the field Turing's famous test belongs to

explanation.surface: Alan Turing starts to make sense of German codes with some clever machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: Turing broke the Nazis' ciphers and wrote the test for machine intelligence, so every word of the surface is true of him — and the definition is the one thing that is not.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the person doing the attacking, the one who sets upon somebody, which is what the clause describes.

clue.text: Hotel of inferior quality — not the first in Whitley Bay?

parts.note: H is Hotel in the phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: not means the letter named is left out

parts.note: worse means of lower quality

indicators.note: the first in a word means only its opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the word gives its first letter W

explanation.surface: A shabby hotel in Whitley Bay, a seaside town in north-east England, is criticised.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitley Bay looks like one place; 'Bay' alone is the definition. 'not the first in Whitley' removes W, Whitley's initial, from WORSE, leaving ORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A bay is a horse with a reddish-brown coat, so the question mark marks it as an example.

clue.text: How's your father's leg strain initially? See how far you can push it?

definitions.text: See how far you can push it?

indicators.note: 'Initially' says where a piece goes rather than which letters it is: the strain word is placed at the front of the assembly.

parts.note: to strain at something is to try it, and both words mean testing a thing to its limit
'how's your father' is old British slang for sex, and 'it' is the coy word for the same thing
in cricket the leg side of the field is the on side

explanation.surface: Someone asks after dad's pulled leg muscle and how much more it can take.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How's your father' is old British slang for hanky-panky, which is how the surface can enquire innocently after a torn muscle while the wordplay collects a euphemism.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means chancing your arm — pushing to see what you can get away with before somebody stops you.

clue.text: Man cleared out space in resort and pitches tents

indicators.note: To re-sort is to sort again into a new order, which is what the letters beside it are asked to do.
A room cleared out has nothing left in the middle, so the word keeps only its two end letters.

parts.note: MAN emptied of its middle leaves the two ends
five more letters of fodder, taken as they come

explanation.surface: A man clears out a space at a holiday resort and puts up tents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like the seaside town the surface needs and means re-sort, a second shuffle of the letters — the hyphen it hides is the whole trick.
explanation.definitionFit: An army doing this pitches its tents and settles for the night, one verb covering the whole business of making camp.
